intro.title: How far have you handed your work to AI, and what does that expose you to?
intro.line: You get your level on a five-step scale, the next step up and the risks to fix. About four minutes. Your answers stay in this browser.
aiLines: It asks where you’d put yourself, 1 to 5.
It looks through your memory and past chats for how you use AI.
It shows your level, your risks and your first steps.
intro.copied: Prompt copied. If it isn’t in the chat yet, paste it and send.

around.name: Around you
around.risk: Other people’s AI can copy your voice and face, learn from what you post and decide things about you.

levels.name: Ask
levels.line: You ask AI a question now and then, or not yet.
levels.risk: What you type can be kept and trained on. Answers sound sure even when they’re wrong or just agree with you.

levels.name: Work with
levels.line: You work through tasks with it, back and forth. You make each call.
levels.up: Bring it one real task a week and go back and forth until it’s good.
levels.risk: You share more: work files, health, other people’s details. And it starts doing some of your thinking.

levels.name: Delegate
levels.line: You hand over a whole piece of work and use what comes back.
levels.up: Write a short brief, then hand over the whole first draft.
levels.risk: Its mistakes go out under your name, and skills you stop using fade.

levels.name: Automate
levels.line: It works in your email, calendar or files and runs on a schedule.
levels.up: Connect one source it can read, then schedule one task you repeat every week.
levels.risk: Anything it reads can carry instructions. One email or web page can steer it toward your data.

levels.name: Hand over
levels.line: It runs whole workflows and acts for you. You check results, not steps.
levels.up: Give an agent one whole workflow where mistakes are cheap, with limits it can’t cross.
levels.risk: It acts before you look. One bad step can send, buy or delete for real.

sources.label: Feng, McDonald & Zhang: Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents (2025)
Anthropic: Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice (2026)
Anthropic: How employment is changing at Anthropic (2026)
Mitchell et al.: Fully Autonomous AI Agents Should Not be Developed (2025)

questions.label: Last month
questions.text: What have you done with AI in the last month?

options.label: Asked it a question
options.detail: A fact, an explanation, a translation

options.label: Worked on something with it, back and forth
options.detail: A draft, a plan, an analysis you shaped

options.label: Handed over a whole task and used the result
options.detail: A report, code, slides, with light edits

options.label: Let it into your email, calendar or files
Set it to run on a schedule or trigger
Let it act without checking each step
options.detail: Send, book, buy, change files or code

questions.label: Most weeks
questions.text: Which of these do you do most weeks?
questions.hint: Pick the furthest one. A level is what you do most weeks, not what you tried once.

questions.label: AI assistants
questions.text: Which AI assistants do you use?

questions.label: Personal advice
questions.text: Do you ask them for advice on personal things?
questions.hint: Relationships, health, money, an argument with someone.

options.label: Often
options.note: Chatbots back the user about 50% more often than people do. One instruction helps.

questions.label: AI at work
questions.text: Do you use AI for work?

options.label: Yes, with my own accounts
options.note: Two in three office workers have used AI their employer doesn’t allow. Work files can end up in training data.

questions.label: Checking its work
questions.text: When AI hands you finished work, what do you do before using it?

options.label: Check every fact, number and quote
Read it through
options.note: Errors hide in text that reads well. Courts have logged about 2,000 cases of AI-invented citations.

options.label: Mostly use it as is
options.note: That’s where mistakes get through, and where your own skill fades.

questions.label: What it reaches
questions.text: What can AI get into for you?

options.label: Email or messages
options.note: Email is how outside text reaches your agent. Keep reading and sending apart.

options.label: A browser where you’re signed in

questions.label: Approvals
questions.text: Before it sends, buys or deletes something, does it ask you?

options.label: No, it just goes ahead
options.note: Common with practice: Anthropic saw full auto-approve go from about 20% to over 40% of sessions. Keep a stop for sending, paying and deleting.

questions.label: Panicked call
questions.text: Someone close calls in a panic, in their voice, asking for money now. What happens?

options.label: I ask for our safe word
I hang up and call them back
options.note: Good instinct. A safe word makes it automatic.

options.label: Honestly, I’d probably help
options.note: Most people would. Ten minutes fixes it.

questions.label: Teenagers
questions.text: Do teenagers in your life use AI chatbots or companion apps?
questions.hint: ChatGPT, Snapchat’s My AI, Gemini, companion apps…

options.label: Yes, my own kids
options.note: 72% of US teens have used an AI companion. Controls take fifteen minutes.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Worth asking. 72% of US teens have used one.

questions.label: Bank voice ID
questions.text: Has your bank ever recognised you by voice?
questions.hint: “My voice is my password” or similar.

options.label: Yes, I use voice ID
options.note: Cloned voices have passed these checks. One call turns it off.

questions.label: Voice & face online
questions.text: How much of your voice and face is online?

options.label: Videos or podcasts with my voice
Barely anything
options.note: Your voicemail greeting may still be your voice.

questions.label: Automated decisions
questions.text: Has a company turned you down lately without a clear reason?
questions.hint: A loan, an insurance claim, a job, an account.

options.label: Yes
options.note: You can ask how it was decided, and in some places for a person to look again.
